# Price elasticity of demand

## Summary

The measure of how much the quantity of a good people buy changes when its price changes. Above one in absolute value demand is elastic, below one inelastic. The determinants section lists the availability of close substitutes, whether the good is a necessity, and how much of a buyer's budget it takes. With inelastic demand, a price rise tends to raise total revenue; with elastic demand it tends to lower it.

## Why It Matters

Farid Nasser put it on the reading list of the [[food-business-finance-course]], and I came back to it while preparing the [[price-review-2026]]. It gave me words for what I already suspected: our croissant has few close substitutes in town and costs little against a customer's budget, so a rise should not lose many sales; the plain loaf competes with the supermarket, so it was kept at 5.20 rather than 5.50.

## Key Details

- After the rise, croissant units fell 3% while price rose 13%, which by the article's definition is inelastic (about -0.2) for our counter, at least over six weeks ([[new-prices-launch-2026-03-09]]).
- Revenue rises with price only while demand stays inelastic.

## Caveats

Six weeks of one shop's sales is a rough estimate, and Easter fell inside the window. The theory says nothing about regulars' goodwill.
